Śaivāgamas
------------------------------------------
Āgamas are post-Vedic Hindu scriptures relevant even today. They primarily deal with practical spiritual disciplines, ethical codes and temple rituals.
Of the three main divisions of the आगमस् (See ĀGAMAS.), the शैवागमस् are listed as the first. They are also called by other names such as Saṁhitā and Mahātantra. They had already come into existence by the first century B. C.
Their philosophical tenets are the same as those of the पाशुपत cult (See ŚAIVISM.).
The शैवागमस् are divided into two groups: pradhānāgamas and upāgamas.
The former comprises 28 works and the latter either 208 or 225.
The twenty-eight major आगमस् are:
Acintyāgama, Ajitāgama,
Aṁśumānāgama, Analāgama,
Bimbāgama, Candrajñānāgama,
Dīptāgama, Kāmikāgama,
Kāraṇāgama, Kiraṇāgama,
Lalitāgama, Makuṭāgama,
Niśśvāsāgama, Pārameśvarāgama,
Prodgītāgama, Rauravāgama,
Sāhasrāgama, Santānāgama,
Śarvāgama, Siddhāgama,
Sūkṣmāgama, Suprabhedāgama,
Svāyambhuvāgama, Vātulāgama,
Vijayāgama, Vimalāgama,
Vīrāgama, Yogajāgama.
These major आगमस् have evolved out of the five faces of शिव (= पञ्चानन) as follows:
1. सद्योजात: Kāmika, Yogaja, Acintya, कारण,

. ईशान: Prodgīta, Lalita, Siddha, Santāna, Śarva, Pārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Vātula.

Sometimes, the first ten आगमस् listed under the first two aspects of शिव are named as Śivasaṁhitās and the rest as Rudrasaṁhitās.
All these āgamās follow the standard pattern of the fourfold division, viz., Jñanapāda, Yogapāda, Kriyāpāda and Caryāpāda. (See ĀGAMAS for details.)
Anyone who wishes to practise the disciplines of the शैवागमस् has to undergo दीक्षा or initiation. The process is explained in detail. One interesting point is that it varies according to the गोत्र (lineage) and Vedic śākhā (branch assigned for study) of the seeker, thereby confirming that the शैवागमस् are very much a part of the Vedic tradition.

Śaivism
------------------------------------------
1. Introduction
Śaivism is the religion and philosophy of those who believe that god शिव is the Supreme Being.
Whether रुद्र the Terrible, of the वेदस् and शिव, the Auspicious One, of the ‘non-Vedic’ (‘non-Āryan’) ‘Draviḍian’ cults battled for centuries and then blended to emerge as one deity of compromise—Śiva-महादेव, the Auspicious Great God—is a moot point. As the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन्, which had once been believed to be pre-Āryan, non-Vedic or Draviḍian, came to be accepted as a continuation of the Vedic civilisation itself, in fact its later phase, scholars had to concede that शिव as depicted on some of the seals with a trident and a bull, was very much a Vedic deity even as the मोथेर् Goddess was.
Being the god of destruction and dissolution of the world, as delineated in later literature, शिव had to be रुद्र, the Terrible. Hence supplications to him to be propitious to one’s children (vide Ṛgveda 7.46.2), descendants, cattle and property (ibid., 1.114.8) are quite in order. However, he also has a benign form (Śambhu, the beneficent one), is the heavenly physician who cures one’s diseases and protects one’s cattle.
By the time of the Atharvaveda and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (1.10; 3.2; 4.12,21,22; 3.14; 4.10), the concept had further evolved to indicate him as the supreme or the highest God.
Along with the development of the concept of रुद्र-शिव, there had also been an evolution of the concept and symbology of the लिङ्ग as the chief emblem of शिव. The लिङ्ग resembles a pillar with a semispherical top. Being a rounded surface in all directions, it is, perhaps, the closest approximation to a god considered as beyond all names, forms and attributes. Whereas some scholars find in it the remnants of phallic worship of aboriginal tribes, others feel it is a metamorphosed form of the Vedic yūpastambha (sacrificial post) as the yāgaśālā (sacrificial shed) gradually evolved into the now common Hindu temple. Even if a phallic origin is admitted, a third section of savants argue, there is nothing wrong in it since it represents the generative principle of God, the creator.
Though शैविस्म् might have started as a simple faith and a mode of worshipping Lord शिव as the Supreme Being, over the centuries, it branched off into several varieties of sects and cults. Six of these have left their imprint on the religious history of India though two or three only are surviving and thriving. These may now be considered by arranging them in the English alphabetical order.
2. Kālāmukhas
Based on the fierce descriptions of रुद्र in the वेदस्, some bizarre cults emerged in course of time. The Kālā-mukhas and the Kāpālikas are two such sects worshipping रुद्र-शिव as भैरव and चण्डी.
The Kālāmukhas were so called, probably because they were defacing their faces with black marks and symbols (kāla = black, mukha = face).
Scholars of शैविस्म् consider this sect as a branch of the पाशुपत cult of लकुलीश, also spelt as ‘Nakulīśa’.
These Kālāmukhas (sometimes called ‘ekkoṭi-munis’) had some connections with the descendants of a देवव्रत मुनि of Kashmir. They were quite powerful during the period A.

-1200 in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Kedāreśvara temple of Baḷḷigāve (in the Shimoga district of Karnataka) and the temple town of Śrīśaila (near Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh) were their strongholds. Edicts of the Cāḷukyan kings (11th cent. A. D.) speak of royal patronage to this cult. One of their gurus—Sarveśvara Śaktideva—was the master of 77 temples. They were also well-known for austerity and scholarship.
However, some horrendous practices of theirs, like drinking wine in human skulls, smearing the body with the ashes of crematories, cannibalism and loose morals, made them outcastes in the society.
The teachers of this sect were divided into two groups: राशि and शक्ति.
Rājarājaguru (circa A.

), a well-known कालामुख teacher, was a contemporary of the sage Vidyaraṇya (14th century A. D.).
3. Kāpālikas
Members of a powerful Śaiva sect, the Kāpālikas, were christened as such because they were using a कपाल or human skull, as their begging bowl. They were also wearing a garland of human skulls. They were quite active and powerful during the period 7th century onwards for about 500 years in Śrīśaila (Andhra Pradesh) and some parts of Tamil Nadu like काञ्चीपुरम्, Tiruvoṭriyūr, Melpāḍi and Koḍumbāḷūr. Worship of भैरव and चण्डी, drinking wine, eating human flesh and ash, arming themselves with a mace and promiscuous sex were common among the members of the sect.
According to a work called Śabara-tantra 24 teachers, starting with आदिनाथ and ending with Malayārjuna, have been mentioned. They were fiercely anti-Vaiṣṇava.
4. Kashmir Śaivism
Introduction
Though शैविस्म् is an old religio-philosophical system prevalent in many parts of India, certain erudite and enlightened teachers from Kashmir developed a special brand of the same. This came to be popularly known as ‘Kashmir शैविस्म्’ in the annals of philosophical literature of later periods. However, a more technical and acceptable title has been ‘Pratya-bhijñādarśana’.
Basic Literature
Although the basic literature of Kashmir शैविस्म् is some of the आगमस् like the Svacchanda, the Netra and the Vijñānabhairava, a new class of cardinal works was produced by the later writers. Among them, the following are the principal ones: Śivasūtras (revealed to Vasu-gupta) (9th century A. D.), Spandasūtra of Vasugupta, Spandasūtravṛtti of Kallaṭa (chief disciple of Vasugupta), Śivadṛṣṭi of Somānanda (9th century A. D.) and Īśvarapratyabhijñā of Utpala (A.

-1000) was the most brilliant of the later writers whose Vṛtti on the Īśvarapratyabhijñā of Utpala, and his own independent works Tantrāloka and Paramārthasāra have made him immortal in the chronicles of Kashmir शैविस्म्.
Kṣemarāja (A.

-1025), भास्कर and वरदराज were the other noted writers who have enriched this literature.
Philosophical Tenets in Brief
This system puts forward 36 tattvas or fundamental principles out of which the whole च्रेअतिओन् has evolved. They are divided into three main groups:
Śuddhatattva, Śuddhāśuddhatattva and Aśuddhatattva.
The Śuddhatattvas (pure principles) are five: Śivatattva, Śaktitattva, सदाशिव-tattva, Īśvaratattva and Śuddhavidyā-tattva.
The Śuddhāśuddhatattvas are six: māyā, kāla, niyati, राग, विद्या and कला.
The Aśuddhatattvas are twenty-five. They are: puruṣatattva, prakṛtitattva, बुद्धि, अहङ्कार, मनस्, the five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस्, the five कर्मेन्द्रियस्, the five तन्मात्रस् and the five bhūtas.
These tenets appear to be similar to the ones described in the Advaita Vedānta and the Sāṅkhya systems. But there are some basic differences.
These tattvas or principles may now be taken up one by one.
The fundamental tattva of this system is Śivatattva, generally described as Parasaṁvit or the highest (and pure) चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, the same as the Nirguṇa ब्रह्मन् of the Advaita Vedānta. However, as against the two aspects there—the Saguṇa and the Nirguṇa aspects—there are five in this system.
This Parasaṁvit is the original primeval tattva from which all the other tattvas have emerged. It is eternal and ineffable.
The Śaktitattva is primarily the prathama-spandana or first vibration-product (if we can use such a word) of Parasaṁvit. आनन्द or bliss is its chief characteristic. It is the primary source of all movement in further च्रेअतिओन् and the rise of ‘ahaṁ’ or ‘I-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्’.
Then comes the Sadāśivatattva, a further evolution of the Parasaṁvit, wherein there is an awareness of ‘ahaṁ’ (‘I’) and ‘idaṁ’ (‘this’), the former being more prominent. Since ‘idaṁ’ (creation) is still in an extremely subtle state, सदाशिव may also feel ‘ahaṁ idaṁ’ identifying himself with the च्रेअतिओन् about to be projected.
In Īśvaratattva, the fourth, the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् ‘idaṁ’ (creation) becomes equal in prominence to ‘ahaṁ’ (‘I’).
In शुद्धविद्यातत्त्व, the fifth form of Parasaṁvit, ‘idaṁ’ (creation) becomes more prominent. This is the starting point of the actual process of च्रेअतिओन् or evolution or projection.
These five principles have been named ‘Śaktyaṇḍa’.
The next six principles are called ‘Māyāṇḍa’.
Māyā, the first, is the unique power of शिव, which can make the impossible possible. It is not an illusory power responsible only for इग्नोरन्चे as in Advaita metaphysics. It is the real power by which शिव envelops himself, producing bheda (differences), nāma (names), rūpa (forms) and so on, where they did not exist.
This māyā gives rise to the ‘pañca-कञ्चुकस्’ or five coverings that apparently limit the powers of शिव and make him appear as the jīvātman (individual सोउल्), subject to kāla (time), niyati (cause and effect relationship, law of कर्म), राग (desire and attachment), विद्या (limited knowledge, or अविद्या, इग्नोरन्चे) and कला (limited powers of action).
The next group of principles beginning with प्रकृति is called ‘Prakṛtyaṇḍa’. प्रकृति is the matrix of the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्) in a state of balance. When this balance is upset, the products that gradually emerge are: बुद्धि (discriminative faculty), अहङ्कार (ego-sense, sense of individuation and separation), मनस् (mind, general power of thinking, feeling and willing), the five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (organs of perception, viz., eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin or the sense of touch), the five कर्मेन्द्रियस् (organs of action viz., speech, hands, feet and the two organs of evacuation) and the five तन्मात्रस् (the five subtle elements of earth, water, fire, air and ether or space).
The तन्मात्रस्, by their combination, produce the five महाभूतस् or gross elements. Further च्रेअतिओन् proceeds from them. This group is called ‘Pṛthivyaṇḍa’.
The significant points to be noted in this system are:
Sṛṣṭi or च्रेअतिओन् is the evolution of the शक्ति or power of शिव.
The individual सोउल् in bondage in च्रेअतिओन् is also, really speaking, शिव himself.
The total number of fundamental cosmic principles is 36 and not 25 as in the Sāṅkhya system.
Since the created world is an evolute of शिव, it is not different from him. But, it also appears to have its own separate identity. Hence, this system accepts the theory of bhedābheda (both difference and non-difference) between God (Śiva) and his च्रेअतिओन्.
Similarly, the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्) who is called ‘paśu’ (bound सोउल्) is also शिव himself. By practising pratya-bhijñā (remembrance of his real nature as शिव himself) the जीव can get rid of all āvaraṇas (coverings) and become one with शिव. This is his मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
However, this can be secured only by service to the गुरु (spiritual teacher), listening to the teachings of the śāstras (holy books), reflection on them and the practice of योग. But, the final deliverance can come only by śivānugraha (grace of Lord शिव), technically called ‘śaktipāta’ (descent of Lord’s power).
Ultimately, as per this system, it is शिव who covers himself and becomes the जीव, the bound सोउल्. It is शिव, again, who recognises his real nature and ‘regains’ it as it were.
Thus self-forgetfulness (svātma-vismaraṇa) and self-remembrance (svātma-प्रत्यभिज्ञा) are two scenes in the world-play of शिव!
5. पाशुपत Cult
Introduction
The cult of पशुपति or the पाशुपत cult seems to be an ancient one. The use of words ‘pati,’ ‘pāśa,’ and ‘prasāda’ in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (1.11; 6.9; 3.20), worship of शिव as लिङ्ग, the practice of tying the शिवलिङ्ग on the arm as per the stone edict of the king Pravarasena (A.
), Śivaliṅgas discovered in Cambodia (now Kampuchia) and assigned to the period A.

—all these confirm this belief.
The पाशुपत cult is based mainly on the शैवागमस्, certain पुराणस् and a few minor उपनिषद्स् of the post-Vedic period. Some of the आगमस् are: Kāmika, Ajita, अṁशुमान्, Suprabheda, Svāyam-bhuva, रौरव, Mṛgendra, Pauṣkara and Vātula. The पुराणस् are: Vāyu, Kūrma and Śiva. As for their authoritative nature, they have been considered equal to the वेदस्, the वेदाङ्गस्, the Mahābhārata and the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
The period of the आगमस् ranges from the first century to the fourteenth. They are prevalent mostly in South India, that too in Tamil Nadu. Whether they—some of them at least—were originally composed in Tamil and later rendered into Sanskrit, or were directly written in Sanskrit itself, opinion seems to be divided.
Chief Tenets
The topics dealt with in the पाशुपत literature are technically called Pañcār-thas, the five basic subjects. They are: कारण, कार्य, योग, विधि and duḥkhānta.
KĀRAṆA
Kāraṇa, the primeval cause, is शिव, called ‘Pati’ (Lord) here. Some of his other names are: रुद्र, शङ्कर, Kāla, बल-vikaraṇa, अघोर, Sarva, Śarva, Tatpuruṣa, ईशान, ईश्वर and ब्रह्मा. He is anādi (without beginning or origin), avyaya (indestructible) and the cause of च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and dissolution of the world. He is transcendent as well as immanent. He is compassion unlimited. प्रणव or Oṁ is his best symbol.
Unlike the Vedāntic systems, शिव or ईश्वर is only the निमित्तकारण (efficient cause) of च्रेअतिओन् and not the upādāna-कारण (material cause). Though the jīvas (individual souls) and the world have a separate existence, they are completely under his control. It is due to him that the world and the jīvas undergo changes. However, being a prasādi (one who bestows grace), he is ever compassionate to the jīvas. That is why they can get लिबेरतिओन् by meditating on him.
It may not be out of place to mention here that the पाशुपत system is very much akin to the द्वैत Vedānta system of Madhva (A.

-1276). The only difference is that शिव has taken the place of विष्णु, in this case.
KĀRYA
Kārya is the second of the five basics mentioned above. कार्य is defined here not as an effect, but as that which is asvatantra or dependent, कारण being that which is svatantra or independent. In this sense, ईश्वर or शिव alone is the कारण, the jagat (world) and the jīvas being kāryas since they are dependent upon him.
Though ईश्वर is the कारण, the jīvas, being prodded by him, can also be the kāraṇas in the further process of च्रेअतिओन्. So also प्रकृति or प्रधान which is responsible for further evolution of the world. Hence these two have been called ‘kārya-कारण’.
Evolution of the world from the प्रकृति is the same as in the Sāṅkhya philosophy.
One thing has to be noted here. ईश्वर as the original कारण never gets affected by the evolution of the world whereas प्रकृति which is a ‘kārya-कारण’ does. Two examples can make this concept clear. Lotus blooms when the sunlight falls on it. Iron filings move in the vicinity of a magnet. In these cases, neither the sun nor the magnet is affected though the lotus and the iron filings are. So also, ईश्वर remains unaffected by the evolution of the world through the प्रकृति (and the jīvas).
Among the kāryas, the jīvātman (individual सोउल्) is the most important. He has been called ‘paśu’ since he is subject to ‘pāśa’ (bondage) and sees (‘paśyati’) himself as the body-मिन्द् complex forgetting that he is the spirit, whereas शिव has been declared as ‘Paśupati’ (Lord of paśus).
The पशु or the जीव is eternal, all-pervading and possesses the powers to see (dṛkśakti) and to act (kriyāśakti).
The paśus, depending on their spiritual evolution, are classified into two groups: sāñjana (those attached to the body, the senses and the मिन्द्) and nirañjana (the free souls).
The pāśas or bonds that bind the पशु are called malas or impurities. They are three: आणवमल, मायीयमल and kārmamala.
The impurity that makes the पशु (or जीव) get identified with the limited body though he is really infinite, is आणवमल. The bondage that has been brought about by māyā (the power of ईश्वर) is मायीयमल. Limitations that arise due to past karmas are kārmamala.
With the help of योग, the पशु is able to cleanse himself of all these malas and attain the duḥkhānta state (destruction or cessation of all sorrow and suffering).
YOGA
This takes us to the next subject, viz., योग. योग is defined as the saṁyoga (union) of आत्मन् (paśu) and ईश्वर (Paśupati). It consists in detachment from the comforts and pleasures of the life here and looking upon ईश्वर alone as the sole aim of one’s life. This योग can be achieved either through the grace of ईश्वर or through total surrender to him as the only refuge for a पशु.
Yamas like अहिṁसा (non-violence), ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy), सत्य (speaking the truth in a way that helps living beings), asaṅgraha (non-accumulation of things) are useful sādhanas in योग. So also the niyamas viz., akrodha (conquest of anger), gurusevā (service to the गुरु), शौच (cleanliness), mitāhāra (moderation in eating) and jāgarūkatā (vigilance).
VIDHI
‘Vidhi’ is the fourth in the pañcārthas. It means activities like bhasmasnāna (pouring the holy ash on one’s body), upahāra (deliberately acting in a way that people in general will shun the company of the sādhaka), जप (repetition of शिव’s मन्त्र) and pradakṣiṇā (circumambulation of the शिवलिङ्ग).
DUḤKHĀNTA
Duḥkhānta is the last of the pañcārthas. It means cessation of all sorrow and suffering, the same as मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्. It is achieved by withdrawing the मिन्द् from all objects and directing it towards the Lord पशुपति only. This will result in total surrender to him and living near him (samīpa prāpti). In this मुक्ति, there is no ‘living alone’ (kaivalya, as in the साङ्ख्य-योग systems) or total merging (aikya as in Advaita Vedānta). The पशु will then be in the eternal company of पशुपति.
It is interesting to note that the पाशुपत texts describe the attainment of psychic powers like clairvoyance or clair-audience as a part of duḥkhānta. But they also discourage the योगि from paying attention to them since they can prevent him from attaining लिबेरतिओन् in the ultimate sense.
6. Śaivasiddhānta
Though the word ‘Śaiva-सिद्धान्त’ means the doctrine of शैविस्म् in general, it has come to be particularly identified with the brand of शैविस्म् that has been prevalent in the Tamil country over the last thousand three hundred years. It is more a religion of devotional म्य्स्तिचिस्म् than a systematic and speculative philo-sophy, based on the compositions of the Nāyanmārs or नायनार्स् who were 63 in number and lived during the period 7th to 12th centuries A. D.
The canonical literature of Tamil शैविस्म् as redacted by Nambi Āṇḍār Nambi (A.

) can be given as follows:
Sl. Nos.of the books Authors Period A.

and 3 Tirujñāna Sambandhar 7th cent.
4, 5 and 6 Tirunāvukkarasar 7th cent.
7. 1 Sundarar 9th cent.
8. Māṇikkavācagar (Works—Tiruvācakam andTirukkovai) 3rd or 9th cent.
9. Nine different saints (Works—Tiruviśaippā and Tiruppallāṇḍu) 900-1100
10. Tirumūlar (Work— Tirumandiram) 6th cent.
11. Miscellany of poems by saints Pattinattār, Karaikkāl Ammaiyyār and others.
12. Sekkilar (Work—Periyapurāṇam) 12th cent.

The first attempt at a systematic presentation of Tamil शैविस्म् was by मेय्कण्डार् (13th cent. A. D.) in his well-known work Śivajñānabodham, a short treatise of 12 aphorisms. It seems to be a translation in Tamil, of a sanskrit original.
Next in importance, considered a classic in Tamil शैविस्म्, is the work Śivajñāna-śittiyār by Aruṇandi, a disciple of मेय्कण्डार्. This work along with its numerous commentaries is most widely read even now. The Śivajñānabodham mentions and defines the three basic concepts—Pati, पशु and pāśa—deals with the sādhana for the पशु to realise Pati and the phala or spiritual fruit that accrues to him.
The philosophy of शैवसिद्धान्त is very similar to that of the पाशुपत cult, the only difference being that the former accepts 36 basic principles (like Kashmir शैविस्म्) whereas the latter only 25.
7. Vīraśaivism
Introduction
Vīraśaivism, also known as the Liṅgāyata Religion or Sect, is a variant of शैविस्म् found mostly in the Karnataka region of South India. Though the more orthodox sections claim that it is an ancient religion originating from some mythical teachers like Revaṇārādhya, Maruḷārādhya, Paṇḍitārādhya and others, there are others who are inclined to treat it in a figurative sense. For all practical purposes, बसवेश्वर (d. A.
), also known as Basavaṇṇa or Basava, who was the prime minister of the king Bijjaḷa (who ruled from A.

to 1167) was the chief organiser and reformer (if not the founder) of this sect.
A galaxy of saints (numbering more than 300) of this sect like अल्लम प्रभु and Cannabasavaṇṇa, and women-saints like Akkamahādevī have enriched the Liṅgāyata Movement. They revolutionised the religio-social fabric of their times.
Principal Dogmas
A special feature of वीरशैविस्म् is the supreme importance, reverence and worship given to the शिवलिङ्ग or लिङ्ग as the sole emblem of God शिव. Hence the appropriateness of the name ‘Liṅgāyata’ (‘a religion that considers the लिङ्ग as the chief support or basis’). After receiving it from a qualified गुरु in दीक्षा or initiation, it should be worn on the body always, thereby purifying every part of the body.
The chief tenets of this faith are: शिव is the Supreme God. The लिङ्ग is his chief symbol or emblem. The पञ्चाक्षरी-मन्त्र, namaśśivāya, is the redeeming spiritual formula. पञ्चाचारस् and aṣṭā-varaṇas are the main code of conduct. शक्तिविशिष्टाद्वैत is the philosophy behind this system.
As for the process of evolution of the world, the same 36 tattvas or principles given by Kashmir शैविस्म् have been adopted here also.
Practical Disciplines
But for the three malas or impurities (viz., आणवमल, मायीयमल and kārma मल explained earlier), the जीव or पशु (the individual) would have been as wise as शिव, the Pati. In order to get rid of these malas, the individual has to take दीक्षा (initiation) from a duly qualified गुरु. दीक्षा is a simple ritual in which the गुरु worships a लिङ्ग and then ties it round the neck of the disciple which will hang like a necklace. The लिङ्ग is usually encased in a small silver casket. By this process, the गुरु gives the मन्त्र (namaśśivāya) and also transmits his spiritual power.
Women also are entitled for दीक्षा in this cult.
One who is thus initiated is expected to practise the five disciplines known as पञ्चाचारस् and also protect himself with eight ‘coverings,’ the अष्टावरणस्, stipulated by the system.
The पञ्चाचारस् are:
Liṅgācāra—Worshipping daily, the लिङ्ग given to him in दीक्षा.
Sadācāra—Earning money by a virtu-ous profession and utilising the savings for serving the needy, including the jaṅgamas (itinerant preachers).
Śivācāra—Treating all liṅgāyats equally as if they are शिव himself.
Bhṛtyācāra—Cultivating humility towards शिव and his devotees.
Gaṇācāra—Zealously guarding one’s religion, protesting against dis-respect to one’s God and religion as also not tolerating cruelty to animals.
The अष्टावरणस् are:
Guru—Faith and respect towards the गुरु.
Liṅga—Treating the लिङ्ग with reverence and devotion.
Jaṅgama—Respectful treatment of the अस्चेतिच्स् and mendicants.
Pādodaka—Purifying oneself by drinking or sprinkling oneself with the water, with which गुरु’s or a जङ्गम’s feet have been washed.
Prasāda—Accepting ड़ोओद् sanctified in worship.
Bhasma—Wearing holy ash on the forehead and other parts of the body as prescribed.
Rudrākṣa—using a रुद्राक्ष rosary for जप and also wearing it on the body.
Mantra—Repetition of the pañcā-kṣarī-मन्त्र (namaśśivāya) as directed by the dīkṣāguru.
Since the five ācāras and the eight āvaraṇas purify a vīraśaiva (or liṅgāyata) by burning up all his impurities, there is—theoritically—no need for him to observe sūtakas (ceremonial impurities) or cremate his body after death. Hence it is buried.
The Doctrine of शक्ति-viśiṣṭādvaita
Like the viśiṣṭādvaita of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137), the viraśaivas also accept a viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy, which, however, is a little different. In Rāmānuja’s system, ब्रह्मन् is advaita (one without a second), but qualified (viśiṣṭa), since he has प्रकृति (acit) and the jīvas (cit) in himself, as inseparable entities. However, in वीरशैविस्म्, the viśiṣṭatva (being ‘qualified’) is confined only to his शक्ति or power, with the help of which च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and dissolution of the world take place. ब्रह्मन् or God and his शक्ति are non-different, even as heat is from fire or light from the sun. And, ब्रह्मन् is always conscious of his power. Thus here, viśiṣṭatva implies only विमर्श or self-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the inherent power. Hence the name शक्ति-viśiṣṭādvaita for this system.
The Doctrine of Ṣaṭsthala
In वीरशैविस्म्, शिव or ब्रह्मन् or God is called ‘Sthala’. He is ‘Sthala’ because he, like the sky or space (sthala = space) is limitless or infinite. Also the word ‘sthala’ can, etymologically, mean that from which the world emerges and evolves, in which it is stationed and into which it gets dissolved (stha = being stationed; la = getting dissolved).
According to the doctrine ‘Ṣaṭsthala-सिद्धान्त,’ शिव divides himself into two aspects, लिङ्ग and अङ्ग, the former being himself and the latter, the जीव. Both these, again, divide themselves into three further aspects; लिङ्ग into इष्टलिङ्ग, प्राणलिङ्ग and bhāvaliṅga; अङ्ग into tyāgāṅga, भोगाङ्ग and योगाङ्ग.
When the जीव renounces his attachment to worldly objects, he is called ‘tyāgāṅga’ and the लिङ्ग given to him by his गुरु at the time of दीक्षा or initiation is the ‘iṣṭaliṅga’ which is the means of his upāsanā or worship. When due to the upāsanā of the इष्टलिङ्ग he is purified, then he enjoys the things of the world as the grace of शिव, becomes ‘bhogāṅga’ and experiences the ‘prāṇaliṅga’ (Śiva’s presence in his heart). When he progresses further, to very high states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in the sahasrāracakra, he is called ‘yogāṅga’ and enjoys highest bliss by his identity with शिव, now called ‘bhāvaliṅga’.
Conclusion
Vīraśaivism, rooted in the ancient शैविस्म्, was nourished by a galaxy of saints. Its active propagation of social equality, its stress on work—not only as a social obligation but also as a part of one’s spiritual evolution—earned for itself a large number of followers. Even though the social revolution part of it has gradually fizzled out (mainly due to the rigidity of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् that still has a sway over the Hindu society), the other aspects of its religio-philosophical system have certainly enriched हिन्दुइस्म्.
8. Epilogue
Like the two important cults of विष्णु and शक्ति (or देवी), the cult of शिव (or शैविस्म्) also has contributed significantly to the ethos and spiritual grace of हिन्दुइस्म्. Rooted in the वेदस् and nourished by the secondary scriptures like the आगमस् and the पुराणस्, शैविस्म् has grown into a widely accepted and popular religious system, well-integrated with other systems, sects and subsects within हिन्दुइस्म्.
